Class ProcessingContext

java.lang.Object
be.imgn.gaia.processing.ProcessingContext
public final class ProcessingContext extends Object
Everything a processor works with: javac's processing environment, and gaia's helpers on top of it.

A StepProcessor creates one and passes it to its steps. Any processor can create one with of(ProcessingEnvironment, Class).

    • type

      public TypeMirror type(Class<?> clazz)
      Returns the type of a class, as the compilation sees it: a primitive type for int.class, the void type for void.class, an array type for String[][].class, and a declared type for a class, interface, enum, record or annotation type, nested ones included, such as Map.Entry.class.

      A generic class gives its raw type: List.class gives List, neither List<E>, the type of its declaration, which TypeElement.asType() gives, nor any parameterization of it, which type(Class, Class...) and type(Class, TypeMirror...) build. So does an inner class of a generic class: Outer.Inner.class gives the raw Outer.Inner.

      The compilation finds the class by its canonical name, on its own class path or module path, which need not be those the processor runs with.

      Parameters:
      clazz - the class, which may be primitive, void or an array
      Returns:
      its type
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if the class has no canonical name, as a local, anonymous or hidden class, or if the compilation cannot see it

    • type

      public DeclaredType type(Class<?> clazz, Class<?>... typeArguments)
      Returns a parameterized type of a generic class, with classes as type arguments: type(Map.class, String.class, Integer[].class) gives Map<String, Integer[]>. To pass other types, such as a parameterized type, a type variable or a wildcard, as type arguments, use type(Class, TypeMirror...).
      Parameters:
      clazz - the generic class or interface
      typeArguments - as many type arguments as clazz has type parameters, each a class or an array class; none for the raw type
      Returns:
      the parameterized type, or the raw type for no type arguments
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if clazz or a type argument has no canonical name or is not visible to the compilation, if clazz is primitive or an array, if a type argument is primitive, if the number of type arguments is not that of the type parameters of clazz, or if clazz is an inner class of a generic class: see type(Class, TypeMirror...)

    • type

      public DeclaredType type(Class<?> clazz, TypeMirror... typeArguments)
      Returns a parameterized type of a generic class, with any reference types or wildcards as type arguments: 
      // Map<String, List<? extends Number>>
WildcardType numbers = context.types().getWildcardType(context.type(Number.class), null);
DeclaredType map = context.type(Map.class, context.type(String.class), context.type(List.class, numbers));

      No type arguments give the raw type, as type(Class) does. Type arguments are not checked against the bounds of the type parameters: type(Enum.class, String.class) gives Enum<String>.

      The type arguments of a generic inner class of a generic class, such as Outer<O>.Inner<I>, go with those of the class it is in: build it with Types.getDeclaredType(DeclaredType, TypeElement, TypeMirror...), from the parameterized enclosing type, as Outer<String>. A generic static nested class, or a generic inner class of a class that is not generic, has no such constraint.

      Parameters:
      clazz - the generic class or interface
      typeArguments - as many type arguments as clazz has type parameters: declared types, array types, type variables, wildcards, or types javac could not resolve; none for the raw type
      Returns:
      the parameterized type, or the raw type for no type arguments
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if clazz has no canonical name or is not visible to the compilation, if it is primitive or an array, if a type argument is another kind of type, such as a primitive type, if the number of type arguments is not that of the type parameters of clazz, or if clazz is an inner class of a generic class

    • isSameType

      public boolean isSameType(TypeMirror left, TypeMirror right)
      Returns whether two types are the same type, ignoring type annotations: @Nullable String is the same type as String, and so are List<@Nullable String> and List<String>, @Nullable T and T, or String @Nullable [] and String[], at any depth, wildcard bounds included.

      This is Types.isSameType(TypeMirror, TypeMirror), which javac implements ignoring type annotations, except for wildcards. Types.isSameType says that a wildcard is never the same type as any type, itself included, while javac compares the wildcards of type arguments by their bounds. This compares two wildcards the same way: ? extends Number is the same as ? extends @Nullable Number, ? super String as ? super String, and ? as ? extends Object, as List<?> is the same type as List<? extends Object>; a wildcard is never the same type as a type that is not a wildcard.

      Otherwise, types are the same as Types.isSameType says: a raw type, such as List, is neither the same type as a parameterization of it nor as the type of its declaration, List<E>; a type variable is only the same type as itself, not as another type variable of the same name; and a type javac could not resolve, of kind TypeKind.ERROR, is the same type as any type, so check for those first.

      Parameters:
      left - a type
      right - another type
      Returns:
      true if left and right are the same type

    • asSupertype

      public Optional<DeclaredType> asSupertype(TypeMirror type, TypeElement supertype)
      Returns a supertype of a type as that type sees it, with the type arguments its hierarchy gives it. With class StringConverter extends AbstractConverter<String> and class AbstractConverter<X> implements Converter<X>, the Converter supertype of StringConverter is Converter<String>; that of a field of type ArrayList<Integer>, as an Iterable, is Iterable<Integer>. A type is its own supertype.

      Type arguments are substituted as they are, without capture: a type variable or a wildcard that the type leaves open stays in the result, as Converter<X> for AbstractConverter<X> itself, or Iterable<? extends Number> for List<? extends Number>. A raw type, or a hierarchy that goes through a raw supertype, as class Legacy implements Comparable, gives a raw supertype, without type arguments. A type variable or an intersection type has the supertypes of its bounds. A type javac could not resolve has no supertypes, and the supertypes it could not resolve contribute nothing.

      The type arguments of the supertype are the answer to "what is T of Converter<T> for this type?": 

      Optional<TypeMirror> converted = context.asSupertype(element.asType(), converter)
        .map(supertype -> supertype.getTypeArguments().getFirst());
      Parameters:
      type - the type: a declared type, a type variable or an intersection type
      supertype - the class or interface to find among the supertypes of type
      Returns:
      the parameterization of supertype that type is a subtype of; empty if it is not a subtype of it, or if it is another kind of type, such as a primitive, which is not boxed, or an array

    • methods

      public List<ExecutableElement> methods(TypeElement type)
      Returns the methods of a type as the compiler sees them: those it declares, and those it inherits from its supertypes, as JLS 8.4.8 and 9.4.1 define inheritance. A method that the type, or another inherited method, overrides is left out, as is a static method it hides. Private methods of supertypes, static methods of interfaces, and package-private methods of another package are not inherited. An interface also has the public methods of Object it does not override, which JLS 9.2 makes its members.

      A type can inherit several methods with override-equivalent signatures, such as an abstract method of its superclass and one of an interface: they are all returned. abstractMethods(TypeElement) keeps one.

      The methods are those of the type's declaration, with its type variables: as a member of a parameterized type, a method has the types types().asMemberOf(type, method) gives, which is what Method.overriding(ExecutableElement, DeclaredType, Types) uses. Supertypes javac could not resolve contribute nothing.

      Whether a method overrides another depends on the type both are members of, which elements().overrides(overrider, overridden, type) takes: Elements.overrides(ExecutableElement, ExecutableElement, TypeElement). A concrete method of a superclass implements, as seen from a subclass, an interface method that the subclass implements and the superclass does not: with class Base { public void run() {} } and class Task extends Base implements Runnable {}, Base.run() overrides Runnable.run() from Task, but not from Base, which is why Runnable.run() is not among the methods of Task. A method does not override itself; a static method does not override, but hides; and a package-private method is not overridden from another package.

      Parameters:
      type - the class, interface, enum, record or annotation type
      Returns:
      its methods, without constructors or initializers: those it declares in the order of TypeElement.getEnclosedElements(), then those it inherits from its superclass, then from each of its direct superinterfaces in turn, each in the order this method returns for that supertype; each method once; for an interface, the methods of Object last

    • abstractMethods

      public List<ExecutableElement> abstractMethods(TypeElement type)
      Returns the abstract methods a type leaves to its implementations: the abstract ones among its methods. A default method is not abstract, unless a subinterface declares it again as abstract; an abstract method that a superclass implements, or that a public method of Object implements for an interface, such as Comparator.equals, is not returned.

      Of several abstract methods with override-equivalent signatures, which one method implements all at once, only one is returned: the first whose return type can be returned for all of them and whose thrown exceptions all of them allow; failing that, the first whose return type can; failing that, the first.

      To implement them, as a class implementing an interface or extending an abstract class: 

      DeclaredType supertype = (DeclaredType) element.asType();
for (ExecutableElement method : context.abstractMethods(element)) {
    implementation.addMethod(Method.overriding(method, supertype, context.types())
            .addStatement("throw new $T()", UnsupportedOperationException.class)
            .build());
}
      Parameters:
      type - the class, interface, enum, record or annotation type
      Returns:
      its abstract methods, in the order of methods(TypeElement); empty if it has none, as for a concrete class

    • isFromSource

      public boolean isFromSource(Element element)
      Returns whether an element comes from a source file of this compilation, and so is compiled with the code a processor generates, rather than read from a class file compiled before. The sources are those given to javac, those it finds on its source path, and those a processor generated, in any round. A type of a library, on the class path or the module path, of the platform, or compiled by an earlier build and found again in the class output, does not; nor does a class file a processor generated. 
      if (context.isFromSource(dependency)) {
    // compiled now: generate its factory too
} else {
    // compiled before: read what its class file declares
}

      The answer is the same in every round, the last one included, unlike the root elements of a round, which are only the types new in that round: an element held back to a later round, or the types it refers to, are found this way whatever round they come from.

      An element declared in a type, such as a nested or local type, a method, a field, a parameter or a type parameter, comes from the file of its top-level type. A package comes from its package-info.java and a module from its module-info.java: a package without one, or the unnamed module, comes from no file.

      Parameters:
      element - the element
      Returns:
      true if the element comes from a source file of this compilation; false if it comes from a class file, or from no file javac knows of, as a type javac could not resolve
      Throws:
      UnsupportedOperationException - if the compiler does not implement Elements.getFileObjectOf(Element), as javac does

    • forEach

      public <T> void forEach(Iterable<? extends T> items, Consumer<? super T> action)
      Runs an action on each item in turn, typically an element, reporting a ProcessingException the action throws for one item as an error, with Diagnostics.error(ProcessingException), and going on with the next item. Validation can then throw at the first problem it finds with an element without stopping the others: 
      context.forEach(elements.annotatedWith("com.example.Mapper"), mapper -> {
    if (!mapper.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.PUBLIC)) {
        throw new ProcessingException("must be public", mapper);
    }
    // generate the mapper
});

      Any other exception stops the iteration and propagates.

      Type Parameters:
      T - the type of the items
      Parameters:
      items - the items, such as the elements a step gets
      action - what to do with each item

      public Optional<AnnotationReader> annotation(Element element, String qualifiedName)
      Returns a reader of the annotation of a type written on an element. A repeatable annotation written several times is only found through its container: see annotations(Element, String).

      An annotation of a type javac could not resolve, such as @Missing or @com.example.Missing when no such type exists, is never found, not even by the name it is written with: as for the other lookups, its type is unknown, and so are its elements. Annotations are not inherited: see inheritedAnnotation(TypeElement, String).

      Parameters:
      element - the annotated element
      qualifiedName - the fully qualified name of the annotation type
      Returns:
      a reader of the annotation, or empty if the element does not have it

    • annotations

      public List<AnnotationReader> annotations(Element element, String qualifiedName)
      Returns readers of every annotation of a type on an element, whether it is written once, several times, or within its container. Javac wraps the annotations of a repeatable type written several times in their container, the type @Repeatable names, so that the element only has the container, which annotation(Element, String) finds by the container's name only. This looks into the container, as AnnotatedElement.getDeclaredAnnotationsByType(Class) does: with @Repeatable(Tags.class) @interface Tag, the Tag annotations of @Tag("a") @Tag("b") and of @Tags({@Tag("a"), @Tag("b")}) are @Tag("a") and @Tag("b").

      The language forbids an annotation written several times next to its container, but allows it written once next to its container, as in @Tag("a") @Tags({@Tag("b"), @Tag("c")}): the annotation and those the container wraps are all returned, in the order they are written, here a, b, c. A container that is itself repeated, in the container of the container, is not looked into. Annotations of a type javac could not resolve are not returned. Annotations are not inherited: see inheritedAnnotation(TypeElement, String).

      Parameters:
      element - the annotated element
      qualifiedName - the fully qualified name of the annotation type
      Returns:
      readers of the annotations of that type on the element, in the order they are written; for an element read from a class file, javac reads the annotations kept at run time before the others, so the order is that of the source among annotations of the same retention; empty if the element has none

    • annotationsAnnotatedWith

      public List<AnnotationReader> annotationsAnnotatedWith(Element element, String metaAnnotation)
      Returns readers of the annotations of an element whose type is annotated with a meta-annotation: with javax.inject.Qualifier, the JSR-330 qualifiers of the element, such as @Named("primary"). Only the meta-annotations of the annotation type itself count, as for qualifiers and scopes; annotationsMetaAnnotatedWith(Element, String) also follows the meta-annotations of meta-annotations.

      The annotations considered are those annotations(Element, String) sees: a container of a repeatable annotation, and each annotation it wraps, so that the repeated annotations of a meta-annotated type are found although only their container is written on the element. The meta-annotation may itself be repeated on the annotation type. The meta-annotation written on the element is not returned, unless its type is annotated with itself. Annotations of a type javac could not resolve are neither returned nor followed.

      Parameters:
      element - the annotated element
      metaAnnotation - the fully qualified name of the meta-annotation type
      Returns:
      readers of the annotations whose type has the meta-annotation, in the order they are written, each container followed by the annotations it wraps; empty if there is none

    • annotationsMetaAnnotatedWith

      public List<AnnotationReader> annotationsMetaAnnotatedWith(Element element, String metaAnnotation)
      Returns readers of the annotations of an element whose type is annotated with a meta-annotation, directly or through other annotations, at any depth: with @Component @interface Controller and @Controller @interface RestController, both @Controller and @RestController are meta-annotated with @Component. annotationsAnnotatedWith(Element, String) only looks at the annotation type itself.

      Each annotation type is examined once for an annotation, so that cycles end: @Documented annotates itself, and @Retention and @Documented annotate each other. The annotations considered, on the element and on the annotation types, are those of annotationsAnnotatedWith(Element, String). The meta-annotation written on the element is not returned, unless its type is meta-annotated with itself, as through a cycle.

      Parameters:
      element - the annotated element
      metaAnnotation - the fully qualified name of the meta-annotation type
      Returns:
      readers of the annotations whose type has the meta-annotation at some depth, in the order they are written, each container followed by the annotations it wraps; empty if there is none

    • inheritedAnnotation

      public Optional<AnnotationReader> inheritedAnnotation(TypeElement type, String qualifiedName)
      Returns a reader of the annotation of a type that a class has, declared on it or inherited from a superclass, as @Inherited makes it present: if the class does not declare one, and the annotation type is @Inherited, the nearest superclass that declares one gives it. Only classes inherit annotations, and only from their superclasses: never from the interfaces they implement, and an interface inherits nothing. Methods and other elements do not inherit annotations, not even from the methods they override: annotation(Element, String) reads theirs.

      This builds on Elements.getAllAnnotationMirrors(Element), which gives every annotation present on an element, inherited ones included. A superclass javac could not resolve gives nothing, nor do its superclasses. A repeatable annotation written several times is stored in its container, which the language requires to be @Inherited too: the class declares or inherits the container, so look it up by the container's name.

      Parameters:
      type - the class, or another type, which only has the annotations it declares
      qualifiedName - the fully qualified name of the annotation type
      Returns:
      a reader of the annotation the type declares, or else the one it inherits; empty if it has none
